# Functional Programming Scala Laboratories

A fragmented set of Scala exercises rebuilt as one coherent laboratory. Scala **3.3.8 LTS**
on **JVM 21**, production code on the standard library alone, **33 deterministic MUnit
tests**.

Seven modules, each answering one question, mapped to their implementation and their test
evidence in `docs/CONCEPT_MAP.md`.

## Why a rewrite rather than a cleanup

The archive contains repeated downloads, committed build output, partial solutions,
Scala 2-era application patterns, unchecked casts, and actor examples whose correctness
depends on `sleep` and console timing. Copying it forward would have preserved the
ambiguity rather than resolved it — see [[clean-room-rebuild-from-specification]] for the
general rule, though here it is a quality decision rather than a provenance one: the
material is the author's own.

What carried across is the list of learning goals. Everything else was written anew.

## The seven stops

| Module | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| `Recursion` | total APIs, tail recursion, `BigInt`, Euclid's algorithm |
| `FunctionalList` | a recursive ADT with folds, maps, filters, type-safe sorting |
| `ImmutableCollections` | order-preserving transformations over standard collections |
| `Expr` | an expression ADT with an `Either` evaluation boundary |
| `Tree` | structural recursion, folds, mapping, mirroring, traversal |
| `TeamMember` | accumulating validation without exceptions or partial objects |
| `DeterministicConcurrency` | parallel execution with input-ordered results |

`TeamMember` is the one worth reading. Validation that **accumulates** returns every
failure at once instead of the first, and never constructs a half-valid object to carry
the errors — which is the failure mode of the exception-based version, where the object
exists before anyone has checked whether it should.

## Guarantees, and why each is a guarantee

**Expected failures are `Either` or a validated result** — never `null`, an unchecked cast,
or a sentinel number. The archive contained all three, and each one is a failure the type
system was offering to catch for free.

**Collection APIs preserve input order** unless the name says `sort` or `reverse`. An
ordering that happens to hold is an ordering callers will depend on and maintainers will
break.

**Concurrent results line up with input positions** even though tasks finish in any order.
This is the direct answer to the archived actor examples: their correctness depended on
timing, so the tests could only be flaky or vacuous. Making completion order irrelevant to
the result is what makes a deterministic test possible at all.

**No wall-clock timing, randomness, network, or shared global execution context in tests.**
A test that sleeps is a test that is slow when it passes and wrong when it fails.

## Verification

```bash
scala-cli test .
scala-cli run . --main-class fplab.runLaboratories
```

`scripts/verify-toolchain.ps1` checks the pins are the pins actually installed, and
`scripts/verify-layout.ps1` checks the structure — both run in CI on a clean Java 21
runner alongside compile, test and demo. Pinning a version in a build file and never
asserting it is how a project comes to require a toolchain nobody documented.

### 2026-08-12 reference audit

The layout verifier passed with **16 Scala files**, no archived artifacts, and no exact
duplicate sources on Java 21. The local runner did not expose `scala-cli`, so no compile,
test, or demo result is claimed from this environment. The existing transit-map visual is
kept as a guide to the documented seven modules and 33 declared deterministic MUnit tests;
the unverified count remains explicitly attributed to the repository, not this audit.
